snippet.title: Icom IC-7110 FCC Approved: What the Filing Actually Reveals
snippet.description:
The Icom IC-7110 just got FCC approval. Here's what the filing actually tells us, what it doesn't, and some pure speculation on when it might reach the US and what it might cost.
The IC-7110 FCC filing: https://fccid.io/AFJ455900

The FCC granted the IC-7110 on November 6, one day after Icom filed. Most of the radio has been public since the Tokyo Ham Fair reveal on August 29, so James (K8JKU) goes through the few details the filing adds: the US ham bands from 160 meters through 70 centimeters, the receive coverage, dual-band Wi-Fi, the Bluetooth 5.3 module and its profiles, and a GPS mention in the test report that Icom hasn't talked about. Then, using the Icom ID-5200's path from approval to delivery as a yardstick, he takes a guess at a ship window and a US price. Both are complete speculation built on unverified numbers. Icom has not announced a US price or ship date.

00:46 What the FCC filing confirms
02:18 What's still confidential
02:32 Ship timing speculation: the ID-5200 comparison
02:51 US price speculation
03:28 Wrap-up

Sources:
- IC-7110 FCC filing and exhibits (attestation letter, scanner report, RF exposure report, antenna report): https://fccid.io/AFJ455900
- Icom America IC-7110 pre-release info (bands, power, touchscreen, D-STAR): https://www.icomamerica.com/media_and_promotions/news/4717/
- The ID-5200 timeline comes from Rory's (W8KNX) own order. The price and ship date are our own estimates, not sourced figures.

snippet.title: Xiegu G7250 Deep Dive: Release Firmware Menus and Settings on Day 1
snippet.description:
An unedited, in-depth look at the Xiegu G7250 on release firmware: every menu, control and setting as it ships on day one. This is the deeper dive after our unboxing.  

If you want the initial opinion of N8JRD,  Start at 24:17 - I talk about the things I dislike, the things I like, and opportunities. 

As a reminder, we're still forming initial functional opinions on this unit and a 'review' style discussion with pros and cons is coming.  

Missed the unboxing? Watch it here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o3IvIljMYcA

We purchased this radio ourselves, and the views and opinions in this video are our own. The Radioddity link and code are affiliate, so we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.

Get the Xiegu G7250 at Radioddity and save $15 with code EVERYDAYHAM: https://www.radioddity.com/products/xiegu-g7250?ref=EVERYDAYHAM

Jim (N8JRD) hooks the Xiegu G7250 up to an end-fed half wave and works through the radio hands-on. He covers the two antenna ports and how to switch between them, preamp, attenuator and AGC, direct mode selection, the meters and SWR readout, and the nested multifunction knobs. Then he digs into the built-in 3:1 ATU, the SWR scanner, voice memories, the general menu and its assignable MFK, scope and display settings, audio EQ, and the system and network menus. He also takes a close look at the optional bandpass filters for 80, 40, 20 and 10 meters, and wraps up with his first impressions and where the G7250 sits against other radios around the $1,000 mark.

snippet.title: Ep. 23 – eBay's FCC Rule, Buying Used Ham Gear and Icom ID-5200A After a Month
snippet.description:
Should a brand new ham buy used gear, and does eBay's new FCC rule change the answer? James, Jim and Rory dig into it in Episode 23, along with a month-long check-in on the Icom ID-5200A.

Rory shares how the ID-5200A has settled into his car, what the color display and on-screen keyboard are like to use, and why native APRS is still on his wish list. The crew compares the buzz around the ID-5200A and the Kenwood TM-D750A, Jim's Xiegu G7250 order is on the way from Radioddity, and James talks IC-7110 hopes and a hotel-window CW attempt from New Mexico.

Then it's the news: eBay's FCC requirement for radios that can transmit outside the ham bands, an update on the Amateur Radio Emergency Preparedness Act, ARISS and NASA signing a new four-year agreement for ham radio on the International Space Station, the new POTA site, and a sobering look at a helicopter strike on a radio tower in Florida. The hosts close with how to find a club that fits, what to check before buying at a swap, and how to send in topic ideas.

snippet.title: Xiegu G7250 Unboxing: Gimmick or Game Changer? 100w, Remote Head?
snippet.description:
When we saw the Xiegu G7250 announcement, we had to get our hands on it-- so we ordered one with our own cold-hard-cash, unboxed the thing, and discovered a bit about Xiegu's first foray into the 100w space. Does it deliver as a game-changer, or is the remote head-hype just a gimmick.

We'll check out what's in the box, how it's built, and how it sounds on the air in this first look at the G7250 from Xiegu.

Get the Xiegu G7250 at Radioddity and save $15 with code EVERYDAYHAM: https://www.radioddity.com/products/xiegu-g7250?ref=EVERYDAYHAM

We purchased this radio ourselves, and the views and opinions in this video are our own. The Radioddity link and code are affiliate, so we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.

Jim (N8JRD) opens the first-batch Xiegu G7250, a 100-watt HF radio with a separate 7-inch control head, and goes through everything in the box: the head with its fold-out stand, the multifunction hand mic, the printed manual, and the cables. Then we look at the radio body, including the cooling, the built-in Anderson Powerpoles, two antenna ports, and an Ethernet jack. There is one surprise about how the head connects to the body. We finish with a first on-air test at 100 watts on an end-fed half wave, a noise reduction check, and a first listen to the speaker.

snippet.title: Radioddity HF-010: The 10 Band Vertical That Comes With Everything
snippet.description:
SPONSORED VIDEO: Radioddity sent Everyday Ham an HF-010 Portable HF Antenna kit, so Jim (N8JRD) opened the case, walked every single piece in it, and then took the whole thing to the park for a real POTA activation.
Get the HF-010 and save $15 with code EVERYDAYHAM: https://www.radioddity.com/products/radioddity-hf-010?ref=EVERYDAYHAM

The pitch on the HF-010 is completeness. Everything you need to walk into a park and start calling CQ is already in the bag: whip, ground spike, extension rods, sliding tuning coil, a separate fixed coil for 80 meters, radials on spools, coax on its own winder, a folding tripod, and a few extras Jim didn't expect to find in there. Throw it in the truck with a radio and you're set.

Jim goes through all of it on the table before anything gets assembled, which is the part nobody else seems to cover. What each piece does, why the threads are the way they are, what the sliding coil is actually doing when you move it, and which pieces are built better than he expected. The tuning coil in particular is smooth, enclosed against weather, and quick to move between bands.

Then it goes up at Island Lake Recreation Area, US-3315, for a genuine activation on 20 meters at 100 watts. The SWR number surprised him, and the first contact out of the gate was a park to park all the way into Texas.

He does have two things he'd change about this kit, and one honest warning about a band it claims to cover. Both are in the video.

snippet.title: DIY Digipeater at Detroit's Historic Masonic Temple
snippet.description:
Jay N8QYQ built an APRS digipeater and a Winlink gateway 210 feet up on the Detroit Masonic Temple, and it now covers 93 miles. Here's how he pulled it off.
Detroit Never Goes Silent (send yourself an email over radio): https://jayaho.us/

James (K8JKU), Jim (N8JRD) and Rory (W8KNX) sit down with Jay Aho (N8QYQ), a Detroit ham who came back to the hobby after 20 years and, a year later, closed the APRS coverage hole over downtown Detroit and the I-96 corridor. Jay explains how a childhood friend who manages the Masonic got him in front of the building's trustees, why he intentionally chose a low-gain Diamond X30 at 30 watts and a WIDE1-1 fill-in configuration, and what it took to build a site that runs unattended in an unconditioned radio room: a Raspberry Pi 4 on Dire Wolf for APRS, a hardened Windows mini PC for VARA FM Winlink, a Yaesu FTM-3100 on each node, watchdog scripts, auto-boot after power loss, Google Remote Desktop, LiFePO4 backup and building ground. He also introduces Detroit Never Goes Silent, a lobby exhibit that sends visitors an email over Winlink, and the push to fund an ARPSC station at Detroit's Emergency Operations Center. Up front: Jason KN4AL's 1000th POTA activation, Activate All RI 2026, the new POTA website beta, shack dashboards built with Claude Code, and everything we've learned about the Icom IC-7110 since Tokyo Ham Fair.

snippet.title: Icom IC-7110 Revealed: Our Live Reaction to the X-026 Unveiling
snippet.description:
Icom finally pulled the covers off the X-026 at Tokyo Ham Fair 2026, and we met the IC-7110. 

We stayed up late to watch the reveal live from Japan and reacted to it in real time.

Watch Icom's official unveiling: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u7QGMbUNB2k

James (K8JKU), Jim (N8JRD) and Rory (W8KNX) sit down for a late night watch party as Icom announces the successor to the IC-7100. We take it in as it lands: HF, 50, 144 and 430 MHz all mode, 100 watts on HF and 6 meters, 50 watts on VHF and UHF, a 4.3 inch color touchscreen with a speaker built into the control head, dualwatch across HF and VHF, CW decode, an FT8 preset, dual band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS and remote control software. We also get into what is not there: no APRS in this announcement, no internal tuner, no display output, and no full duplex for the satellite crowd. Then we do what we always do and guess the price, somewhere between $1,999 and $2,600, and argue about when it will actually ship.

snippet.title: Paper QSL Cards: Still Worth Sending?
snippet.description:
The oldest way to confirm a contact is also the only one you can hold. Postage is not cheap and the turnaround is measured in weeks, so why do all three of us still print them?

Watch the full episode: https://youtu.be/HhhoVukJI3s

James K8JKU makes the case for paper: postcard sized, a design of your choosing on the front, the contact details on the back, and a rare chance in this hobby to show a bit of individuality. He prints scenes from places he has actually been, like the Upper Peninsula, and points out that a card doubles as your business card for an eyeball QSO at a hamfest. Jim N8JRD draws the important line underneath all of it, which is that not every method of QSLing counts the same. An eQSL email is a nice thing to receive and some people treat it as junk mail, but it will not earn you Worked All States or DXCC credit. The three of them hold up their own cards, including Jim's with his poodle and Michigan Tech on the front and the W8EDH club card, and talk through the printing options if you want your own. Rory W8KNX closes it out from the other side of the wait, staring at a South Cook Islands contact and an Alaska CW contact that still have not been confirmed and may never be.

QSL Concept, the printer James uses, not sponsored: https://www.qslconcept.com/

snippet.title: QRZ Logbook or Logbook of the World: Where Should a New Ham Start?
snippet.description:
A QRZ logbook takes about five seconds to start. Logbook of the World takes a postcard in the mail. Both are worth having, and the order you do them in matters.

Watch the full episode: https://youtu.be/HhhoVukJI3s

Jim N8JRD, Rory W8KNX and James K8JKU work through where a newly licensed ham should actually begin with online logging. QRZ gets the case for the easy on-ramp: a page already exists for you the moment you are licensed, a logbook is one button away, and because so many operators started there, confirmations come back fast. Then the turn to Logbook of the World, the ARRL system the serious awards run on. It looks and feels like an older site, the callsign certificate and the password that arrives by post are a real hurdle, and the guys are honest that it is the clunkier of the two. Rory puts that in context by explaining what it replaced, which was bundling up paper cards and standing in line at a hamfest for a card checker to verify them. Jim also raises the part people miss, that LoTW is free to set up but claiming awards from it means ARRL membership and per contact fees. Rory closes on the argument that runs through the whole episode: getting your logs uploaded is not only about your own totals, because somewhere out there it is the contact that finally gives someone else a state or a country.

QRZ: https://www.qrz.com/
Logbook of the World: https://lotw.arrl.org/
ARRL LoTW information and setup guides: https://www.arrl.org/logbook-of-the-world

Then the turn to Logbook of the World, the ARRL system the serious awards run on. It looks and feels like an older site, the callsign certificate and the password that arrives by post are a real hurdle, and the guys are honest that it is the clunkier of the two. Rory puts that in context by explaining what it replaced, which was bundling up paper cards and standing in line at a hamfest for a card checker to verify them. snippet.title: Ham2K PoLo Goes Desktop: Windows, Mac and Linux First Look with Sebastián KI2D
snippet.description:
Sebastián Delmont KI2D quit his job to work on Ham2K full time, and two weeks later he had the Portable Logger running on Windows, Mac and Linux.

All the links and ways to support the project: https://polo.ham2k.com/

James (K8JKU), Jim (N8JRD) and Rory (W8KNX) sit down with Sebastián Delmont (KI2D), the developer behind Ham2K Portable Logger, two weeks after he went independent. He lays out the three-month plan he has given himself, shows the new desktop version running live on a Windows laptop, syncs it to James's phone over a QR code on camera, and explains why he threw out the old code base and rewrote PoLo from scratch. He also names the next-generation app for the first time: HaLo, short for Ham2K Logger. Along the way: the pay-what-you-can business model, why open source is an insurance policy for your logs, CAT control plans, a Raspberry Pi style bridge for radio control over Wi-Fi, multi-operator logging for Field Day, a public API for anyone who wants to build on top of Ham2K, and a public beta targeted for mid-August.

snippet.title: Who Tests Tornado Sirens: Amateur Radio Operators keeping YOU Safe
snippet.description:
Ever wonder how those tornado warning sirens actually get tested? On the first Saturday of every month, ham radio volunteers fan out across Oakland County, Michigan to check every siren, and this time Jim (N8JRD) brought a camera.
Want to help test the sirens? Oakland County ARPSC: https://arpsc.com/sirennet.php

It's the 4th of July, but siren test day doesn't take a holiday. Jim rides along for Oakland County's monthly outdoor warning siren test: listening as net control runs check-ins over the radio, watching a siren spin up and sound off (Cash the poodle was not a fan), and then collecting reports from the volunteers stationed at each siren. Every tester confirms three things: the siren rotated smoothly, it sounded for the full three minutes, and it's physically undamaged and clear of obstructions. One siren this round didn't sound at all, which is exactly the point of testing. That one gets reported to the county for repair and a re-test.

Learn more / get involved:
- Oakland County ARPSC siren test net (how to volunteer): https://arpsc.com/sirennet.php
- Oakland County Outdoor Warning Siren System: https://www.oakgov.com/community/emergency-management/need-to-know/alerts/outdoor-warning-siren-system

We finally got the Buddipole BuddiHEX in the air, and our first try was equal parts fun and lessons learned. First impressions from Episode 19: https://youtu.be/m5aILG8IEd0

James picked up the BuddiHEX with the 7m Mastwerks mast for roughly $1,600, and the crew raised it for the first time at Field Day. In this clip: why it took six of us on the guy lines that first go, why it is a special-event antenna more than a grab-and-go POTA setup, how many people you really need to raise it safely, and the cold solder joint on the 6 meter element that we had to fix straight out of the box. We keep it honest, it was not all rainbows, but there is a lot to like, and a lot still to test before any real performance verdict.

snippet.title: Heil BM-17 Unboxing & Review: Is the Reissue Worth $165?
snippet.description:
The bright-yellow Heil BM-17 was a POTA favorite for years, then it disappeared. Now it's back in black, and we put the new single-sided version to the test.

Get the BM-17 at DX Engineering: https://www.dxengineering.com/parts/hls-bm-17s-dy-b

James (K8JKU) unboxes the reissued Heil BM-17 single-sided headset and compares it head to head with Rory's (W8KNX) original, a unit that's been beaten around in his POTA kit for four years and still works. We get into what actually changed on the reissue: the boom going from metal to all-plastic, the new full-swivel design, and that $165 price. Then we put it on the air for a real audio check.

snippet.title: Field Day Reinvented: How to Boost Club Engagement and Community Outreach
snippet.description:
Is ARRL Field Day still worth it? We think it is, if clubs are willing to rethink what it is for. From Episode 19: https://youtu.be/m5aILG8IEd0

In this clip, the South Lyon Area Amateur Radio Club takes Field Day out of the rustic cabin and into town, trading an emergency-prep campout for a community open house at the historic depot. The payoff was not just the score, 1,193 contacts on three stations at 100 watts and nearly double last year, it was the dog walkers, the museum visitors, and the neighbors who stopped to see what ham radio is all about. The lesson for your club: poll your members, set realistic expectations, and make it accessible.

snippet.title: Is Parks on the Air Past Its Prime? An Honest Debate
snippet.description:
Has Parks on the Air already peaked? This clip is from Everyday Ham Episode 18. Watch the full episode here: https://youtu.be/xKMKYlSsglY?si=StD8OCJ-iOcVTrw6

James (K8JKU), Jim (N8JRD), and Rory (W8KNX) tackle the question every activator is quietly asking: is POTA still growing, or has the program hit its plateau? The guys debate whether Parks on the Air is in its twilight or its golden years, why the growth curve is flattening now that most active hams have already tried it, and what the declining solar cycle means for a program built around QRP and portable operating. They also get into why tougher band conditions may push more operators toward CW and FT8, why bringing every tool in the toolbox matters more than ever, and the volunteers and board members working to keep POTA running for the long haul.

Parks on the Air is a volunteer-run organization. If you love POTA, consider donating at https://parksontheair.com

snippet.title: Field Day 2026 Setup Walkthrough: BuddiHex, BandHopper & Larry the Vertical
snippet.description:
A full walking tour of the South Lyon Area Amateur Radio Club's 2026 Field Day site at the historic Witch's Hat Depot in downtown South Lyon, MI. If you're looking for ideas on how to plan, set up, and run your own Field Day, this one's for you.

We moved Field Day into town this year and built the whole site from scratch, right across from the brewery. In this tour, James (K8JKU), Jim (N8JRD), and Rory (W8KNX) walk you through every decision behind the South Lyon Area Amateur Radio Club (N8SL) operation, a 3A entry plus a Get On The Air station, so you can borrow what works.

What you'll pick up for your own site:
- How we laid out antennas across a tight in-town lot: the homebrew "Larry" 40m vertical, our first hex beam in years (the BuddiHEX), and a Spiderbeam mast stacking the BandHopper 4 on 80m over an Aerial-51 off-center fed dipole
- A beginner-friendly GOTA setup (Icom IC-7300 + a visible, easy-to-adjust Buddistick) with a homemade exchange cheat sheet and paper logging sheet to get first-timers over mic fright
- Keeping operators consistent: a matched fleet of Yaesu FTDX10s on N1MM+, networked with a live projector scoreboard so visitors can follow along
- Cheap, effective site safety and public outreach: caution tape on $2 step-in fence posts, explanatory antenna signs, and a "What is Field Day?" welcome booth
- Small-club realities: crew size, ease-of-setup ratings, and why we finally invested in a directional antenna

snippet.title: Raising a BuddiHEX Hex Beam at Field Day 2026 | South Lyon Area ARC
snippet.description:
We'd never built a BuddiHEX before, so we did it live at Field Day. Full first-time assembly here: https://www.buddipole.com/buddihex2.html

Join the Everyday Ham crew and the South Lyon Area Amateur Radio Club (SLAARC) as we unbox and build a Buddipole BuddiHEX 6-band portable hex beam for the very first time during ARRL Field Day 2026, set up at the historic Witch's Hat Depot in Downtown South Lyon, Michigan. This is a long-form club antenna build walkthrough: every wire element, every guy line, the lost hardware in the tall grass, the near-miss with a mast section, and the lessons we learned along the way. If you like honest, in-depth antenna setups from people figuring it out as they go, this one's for you. Final verdict: an 8/10 setup that goes together smoothly once you know the steps, but bring a buddy.

In this video:
Unboxing the BuddiHEX and laying out the pre-tuned wire elements
Setting up the 7m Mastwerks rotating tripod and mast
Leveling the tripod (and when to actually do it)
Attaching the 6 band-specific wire elements to the spreader arms
The lost hook hunt and a re-soldering repair
Guying the mast without snapping a section
Raising the antenna and final thoughts

snippet.title: Has POTA Peaked? Campfires, Community, and the Future of Parks on the Air
snippet.description:
Has Parks on the Air hit its peak? In this episode of Everyday Ham, James (K8JKU), Jim (N8JRD), and Rory (W8KNX) dig into the future of POTA, from the program's explosive growth to what the declining solar cycle means for QRP and portable operators, and why CW and FT8 may matter more than ever as band conditions get tougher. Is POTA in its twilight, or just entering its golden years?

The conversation comes fresh off the Third Annual Michigan POTA Meetup, where the guys spent a weekend camping, activating, and swapping stories around the campfire with about 70 Parks on the Air enthusiasts at Hartwick Pines State Park. They share what makes a regional meetup worth the drive, what actually brings hams together, and how you can find or even start a meetup in your own area, wherever you call home.

Also in this episode: a Hamvention attendance stat correction, shout-outs to Penn (AC8XI) and Rob (N1RWJ), a conversation about POTA board member Mark Torigian (K8MST) and the volunteers keeping the program running, and around the shack updates including Jim's Diamond X300 install, Rory's camper radio setup with the Yaesu FT-891 and FT-8900, and James flashing alternate firmware on his FX-4CR.

snippet.title: SpoolTenna Ultra Review: Is the Pocket EFHW Worth the Upgrade?
snippet.description:
The SpoolTenna just got pocket-sized. James (K8JKU) takes the new SpoolTenna Ultra (ULTRA-EFHW4010) into the field and compares it head-to-head with the original Parks: same 40-10M end-fed half-wave performance, less than half the weight, and small enough to vanish into a pocket.

It's the same antenna electrically (same 49:1 UNUN, same toroid, same 65 ft of wire), but rebuilt around portability with thinner 26 AWG copper-clad steel wire, a fiberglass barrel, and a thermal-vented backboard for higher duty cycle work. James owns and runs both versions, so this is a real upgrade question, not a spec-sheet read.

Inside this review: what's in the box, the spec differences that actually matter, a teardown peek at the matching network, the weight verified on his own scale, the per-unit SWR field test report, deployment and tear-down in about five minutes, and the all-important pocket test. Includes a chat with Brian Young (AJ9T) of SpoolTenna, filmed at Four Days in May (FDIM).

Is it worth the upgrade over the Parks? Here's James's honest take after using both.

snippet.description:
The dust has settled on Dayton Hamvention 2026, and the crew is back at the table to break it all down. James (K8JKU) holds down the home front while Jim (N8JRD) and Rory (W8KNX) recap three days of new gear, new conversations, and one very controversial concept radio.
We dig into what Icom, Yaesu, and Kenwood actually brought to Xenia, why the Icom X-026 mockup divided the community, and whether the long-awaited Kenwood TM-D750A is finally close to hitting the shelves. Plus our honest reactions to the Icom ID-5200, a walk through Four Days in May, and a full report from the flea market (yes, the junk scale is back).

🎙️ In this episode
Hamvention 2026 attendance, vibes, and the cooler weather we actually got. Big thanks to Ray (N9JA) at Icom, John Kruk (N9UPC) at Yaesu, and Don Arnold (W6GPS) at Kenwood for the time and conversations.
The Icom X-026 concept reveal: is it brilliant marketing or a warm helping of nothing? Plus hands-on reactions to the Icom ID-5200 with native APRS, ambient light sensor, integrated GPS, and an interface borrowed from the IC-7300 MK2.
A Kenwood TM-D750A update: FCC approved, firmware still cooking, September target. And a real second-half-of-2026 showdown brewing between the ID-5200 and the TM-D750A.
Four Days in May highlights, including the new Spooltenna Ultra EFHW4010. Plus Begali keys, N3ZN keys, Modern Morse paddles, and the CW corner of the show.
Yaesu DR-3 repeater series and the next chapter of System Fusion. Flex Radio Aurora AU-510 and AU-520 spotted on the shelf, ready to walk out.
